summary:
Pakistan's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 recognises self-perceived gender identity and prohibits discrimination in education, employment, healthcare, housing and access to goods and services. Rules issued under the Act in 2020 added a neutral 'X' marker for administrative documents, and a 2010 Supreme Court order had directed free medical and educational facilities, microcredit schemes and job quotas for transgender people.

Those protections face an unresolved constitutional challenge. On 19 May 2023 the Federal Shariat Court, ruling across 12 shariat petitions, held that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Act, covering the definition of gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles. In its reasoning the court speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women. The provisions remain in force pending appeal. Amnesty International, which had warned the government on 17 May 2023 against adopting amendments that breach human-rights standards, described the verdict as a blow to transgender and gender-diverse people.

Consensual same-sex conduct is criminalised under Penal Code section 377, punishable by two years to life imprisonment. The provision's definition is unclear and it is framed around male-to-male sex; Human Dignity Trust's December 2024 assessment is that only men are criminalised under it. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under birth-sex status falls within the exposure the section describes.

Lethal violence against transgender women is documented and recurring. In November 2024 gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there within a week. In September 2025 police found the bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi. A February 2026 report described a wave of violence that has left transgender Pakistanis afraid to go out, and a night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana in Karachi in which three bullets were fired through a door and the two narrowly escaped. No per-capita rate for violence against transgender people in Pakistan is available in these sources, so the incidents establish a pattern of targeted attacks rather than a measurable risk level.

Protection in custody and at police stations is a documented failure. Justice Project Pakistan's policy brief finds that legal advances have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment, and identifies implementation failure rather than the absence of law as the central problem; it makes recommendations on custody and police safeguards. Transgender people report suspicion and ridicule at police stations.

Healthcare access is another failure point. In 2016 the transgender activist Alisha, aged 23, was shot seven times and left to bleed to death at Lady Reading Hospital in Peshawar while staff argued over whether to place her in the men's or women's ward; men there taunted her friends and asked whether her blood was HIV-positive. Transgender women use hormones and silicone under poor medical conditions without proper equipment or supervision, and sex-change surgery is rarely available in Pakistan. Transgender people also report being turned away at hospitals.

Same-sex partnership has no legal recognition. The Constitution does not mention sexual orientation or gender identity; Part II article 37 pledges to protect marriage and the family and to oppose obscenity, and Part IX article 227 requires all laws to be compatible with Islam as defined by a government-appointed Islamic council. Penal Code article 496 punishes dishonestly going through a marriage ceremony knowing one is not lawfully married with up to seven years' imprisonment. A small clerical body in Lahore, Tanzeem Ittehad-i-Ummat, declared transgender marriages legal under Islamic law in June 2016.

Official hostility to transgender recognition continues. Senator Mushtaq Ahmad has proposed a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control transgender people's official gender identity.

Expression carries its own risk. Pakistani media censors LGBTQ-related news: the website Queerpk.com was blocked in late 2013, and the Pakistani edition of the International New York Times (Express Tribune) left a blank space where a photograph accompanying a same-sex marriage story should have appeared. Penal Code article 292 bans the sale, distribution, exhibition, ownership or importation of 'obscene' books, pamphlets or images; article 294 prohibits 'obscene' public acts, songs, music or poems; article 153 penalises inducing students to political activity that disturbs public order with up to two years' imprisonment; and article 141 designates an assembly of five or more people an 'unlawful assembly' if its common object is to commit any offence. A person living openly as LGBTQ is likely to face treatment from non-state actors including Islamist and terrorist groups.
tangentialFactors:
A foreign government's November 2025 country-policy assessment of Pakistan concludes that transgender and intersex people are protected under the 2018 Act, that the Federal Shariat Court's 2023 declaration that provisions are un-Islamic leaves ongoing legal disputes, and that LGBT+ people are unlikely to face state persecution. That assessment sits alongside documented police-station ridicule, custody abuse and the 2016 hospital death of Alisha, which indicate that state institutions are a site of risk in practice.

The US State Department's 2021 human rights report for Pakistan records that same-sex conduct is criminalised under section 377, that transgender people (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence, and that societal violence and discrimination persist.

Estimates cited in reporting put Pakistan's transgender population at around 500,000, a group facing social exclusion and abuse.

In 2005 a tribal council in the Khyber region ordered a man who had married a fellow tribesman to leave the area or face death.
localsOnly:
Residents report that local communities often deny transgender people basic education and healthcare despite the 2018 Act's prohibitions, and that landlords refuse them housing and employers dismiss them.

Pakistan's HIV epidemic began in 1987. Government estimates from 2004 put nearly 3,000 people living with HIV, while critics suggested 70,000 to 80,000 and UNAIDS reported possibly up to 210,000. A 2009 survey found male and transgender sex workers at high risk, with sex workers lacking access to condoms and little public health education provided.

LGBTQ Pakistanis are generally reluctant to be open about their sexuality for fear of forced marriage, honour killings, humiliation, blackmail or violence. A 2016 article by a young Pakistani man in the UK-based Gay Star News omitted his surname for his security.
outOfScopeNotes:
The appellate status of the Federal Shariat Court's 19 May 2023 verdict is unresolved in the sources: the challenged sections remain in force pending appeal, and it is not sourced whether they will be restored, amended or struck.

The status of the proposed government 'gender re-assignment board' is not sourced beyond its being proposed; no text, timetable or vote is documented.

Whether the 2020 Rules' neutral 'X' marker remains operational in practice after the 2023 verdict is not sourced.

HIV prevalence estimates for Pakistan are contested and span two orders of magnitude, from a 2004 government figure of nearly 3,000 to a UNAIDS figure of possibly up to 210,000; no single figure is reliable.

No per-capita or population-adjusted data on violence against transgender people in Pakistan is available in the sources, so the documented killings cannot be compared with the general homicide rate.
